newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey, Bulgaria discuss energy imports, storage.
newsitem.headline: Turkey, Bulgaria discuss energy imports, storage.

text.p: Turkish and Bulgarian energy officials met on Tuesday to discuss Turkey's electricity import requirements and its plans to use natural gas storage facilities in Bulgaria.
"The amount of electricity we will import a month may be around 300 million kilowatt hours," Turkey's Energy Minister Recai Kutan told journalists ahead of talks with Bulgarian energy officials.

A Bulgarian delegation, headed by Energy Minister Roumen Ovcharov, was scheduled to sign a memorandum of understanding with Turkey later in the day after discussion of electricity supplies and the usage of gas storage facilities.

Turkey is struggling to meet an annual rise in energy demand of 11 percent and to cope with sharp seasonal fluctuations in domestic energy needs, exacerbated in past years by declining gas supplies from Russia during the winter, Kutan said.
Kutan said the planned storage of gas at Bulgarian facilities would help offset these fluctuations, but said their capacity could only be assessed after the talks.
"Probably we will apply to use two of the three or four underground possibilities which we believe exist," he said.
Bulgarian energy officials have said there are plans to expand annual capacity at the country's Chiren natural gas storage plant from one billion cubic metres to 3-4 billion.

They said Turkey's state-run pipeline company Botas had shown interest in the construction of a new underground facility using abandoned salt caverns in the village of Mirovo near the industrial area of Devnya in northeastern Bulgaria.
Kutan said work was also being carried out on increasing usage of Turkey's gas storage facilities in the northern Marmara region, where supplies were dwindling.

The talks with Bulgarian officials were part of a series of discussions held with regional countries on averting an energy shortage since Turkey's Islamist-led coalition came to power four months ago, Kutan said.
He said a third revenue-raising package to be announced by the coalition soon would include a list of existing power stations which the government was seeking permission to bring back into operation.
"At the moment there is no deficit between our capacity and demand," the minister said. Annual energy demand totals 96 billion kilowatt hours compared with generation capacity of 108 billion.
He said a deficit would only arise as a result of faults and necessary repairs in existing power stations.
Turkey, seeking to diversify its energy resources and lessen dependence on oil and coal, signed a gas pipeline agreement with Iran earlier this month under a 23-year, $23 billion deal.
It has already begun buying electricity from its eastern neighbour since August through an existing 25 megawatt (MW) link, whose capacity will be raised to 100 MW early next year.
